def: A Markdown file at a repository root or in a subdirectory holding the repo-specific context and instructions a coding agent needs, with no schema and no required fields.
deeper: The format's own site calls it 'a README for agents' and draws the boundary by audience: a README carries quick starts and contribution guidelines for humans, while this file carries 'build steps, tests, and conventions that might clutter a README or aren't relevant to human contributors.'[^S1] Because there is no schema, nothing validates the file — every quality property in this course is a discipline you apply, not a rule the format enforces.
pitfall: Treating it as configuration that the agent obeys, rather than text that enters the model's context — so a line reading 'never edit this directory' is believed to prevent the edit, when it only makes it less likely.
distractor_rationale: The filename sits at the repo root beside package.json, .eslintrc, and tsconfig.json, all of which are configuration a program parses and enforces. Position and format cue 'config file', and nothing in the name signals that this one is read by a model rather than executed by a tool.

def: Any file whose job is to give an agent persistent context about one specific repository, whatever filename a given tool reads it under.
pitfall: Assuming one filename covers every tool the team uses, so a file that works for the author is invisible to two teammates on different tools.
distractor_rationale: The whole appeal of an open format is 'write it once,' which people hear as 'one file, every tool.' The format standardises the filename and the resolution rule, not every vendor's implementation of them — Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md and needs a bridge.

def: A packaged, portable workflow an agent loads on demand when the work matches it, as opposed to repository context loaded every session.
pitfall: Putting a multi-step procedure that is identical across five repositories into one repository's instruction file, where it loads on every unrelated session and has to be copied to the other four.
distractor_rationale: A team procedure feels repo-specific because it is team-specific, and the two get conflated. Someone who has only ever used the procedure inside one repo has no occasion to notice it would be equally true elsewhere.

def: The check that decides where knowledge belongs: if the text would still be true when copied into an unrelated repository, it is not a fact about this one.
pitfall: Applying the test to a whole section rather than line by line, so a testing section passes as 'repo-specific' when half its lines are portable norms like 'write tests for new behaviour'.
distractor_rationale: Documents are organised by topic, so it feels natural to judge by topic. Splitting a coherent-looking section down the middle feels like vandalism until you notice the two halves have different destinations.

def: The trigger for adding a line: write it when an agent makes the same mistake a second time, rather than in anticipation of mistakes.
pitfall: Writing the file speculatively from a template, producing long aspirational documents whose lines have never been validated against a real failure.
distractor_rationale: Thoroughness reads as diligence, and a comprehensive first draft feels more professional than a four-line file. The cost of unvalidated lines is invisible because nothing announces that a line has never mattered.

def: The property that instruction-file text is context a model weighs, not a control that prevents an action.
deeper: Claude Code's docs put the consequence in operational terms: these files are 'context, not enforced configuration,' and blocking an action 'regardless of what Claude decides' requires a hook instead.[^S5] The AAIF post reaches the same boundary from measurement: the file 'can tell an agent not to touch a file. It can't guarantee that. Real enforcement still belongs to CI, branch protection, and sandboxed execution.'[^S2] The practical rule is to write the line anyway — it is cheap and it helps — while never letting it stand in for a control you actually need.
pitfall: Treating a strongly-worded prohibition as a guarantee, so a rule reading 'never commit to main' is relied on in place of a branch protection rule that would actually prevent it.
distractor_rationale: Emphatic language reads as authority, and in every other repo file a directive is enforced by something. Someone who has only seen the rule honoured has no evidence that it is probabilistic.

def: The tokens an instruction file consumes at the start of every session, whether or not the task needs any of it.
pitfall: Believing the cost is paid once when the file is written, rather than on every run — so a long file feels like a one-time investment instead of a recurring charge.
distractor_rationale: Writing a document is a one-off act, and documentation in every other context is a fixed cost that readers pay only when they open it. The per-session reload is invisible from the author's side.

def: The decline in how reliably each individual instruction is followed as the total number of instructions rises.
pitfall: Reading a violated rule as evidence the file was ignored, rather than as the predictable effect of instruction count on adherence to every rule in the set.
distractor_rationale: A rule that was followed last month and violated today looks like a change in the agent, not in the file. Nobody connects an ignored line to the fifteen lines added since, because those lines are about other subjects.

def: A benchmark that scales keyword-inclusion instructions from 10 to 500 on one writing task to measure how instruction-following degrades with instruction count.
pitfall: Carrying its percentages to repository work — quoting '68% at 500 instructions' as though it predicted adherence to a 40-line AGENTS.md, when the task, the instruction type, and the model generation all differ.
distractor_rationale: A clean number from a real benchmark is quotable and feels more rigorous than a qualitative claim. The setting that bounds it lives in the methods section, which is the part quotations leave behind.

def: A degradation shape where adherence stays near-perfect until a critical instruction count, then drops steeply with rising variance.
pitfall: Concluding from a currently-reliable file that there is headroom to keep adding, when this shape means the last line before the cliff and the first line after it look identical from outside.
distractor_rationale: Flat performance is normally evidence of margin — in most engineering systems, load you cannot detect is load you can afford. A curve that gives no warning before its knee inverts that intuition.

def: A degradation shape where adherence declines steadily and predictably from low instruction counts onward.
pitfall: Assuming this is the shape your tool follows because it is the intuitive one, and budgeting file length against a gradual curve when the tool may follow a threshold or exponential one instead.
distractor_rationale: Linear is the default mental model for any cost — twice the instructions, twice the trouble. It is one of three measured shapes, and the one that happens to be easiest to reason about is not more likely to be yours.

def: A degradation shape with steep loss at low instruction counts, levelling off at a low adherence floor.
pitfall: Writing for a large instruction budget on the assumption that degradation only matters at high counts, when under this shape the damage is concentrated in the first few dozen lines.
distractor_rationale: The word 'exponential' suggests something that gets bad later, as in exponential growth. Here it describes rapid early loss, which is the opposite of the timing the word usually implies.

def: The measured tendency for instructions appearing earlier in a list to be satisfied more reliably than later ones.
deeper: The benchmark computed it as 'the ratio of error rates in the final third of instructions to error rates in the first third,' with a ratio above 1.0 meaning later instructions are violated more.[^S6] The consequence for a file that grew by accretion is direct: appending each new rule to the end steadily buries the newest rules — the ones you needed most recently — in the least reliable position. Treat it as a documented tendency in that benchmark's setting, which gives you a defensible default for ordering rather than a guarantee about your file.
pitfall: Ordering the file by the sequence rules were thought of, which puts recently-added incident rules — usually the expensive ones — at the bottom where adherence is weakest.
distractor_rationale: Appending is the path of least resistance when editing any document, and chronological order feels neutral rather than like a choice. Nothing in the editing experience suggests position carries weight.

def: The assembled sequence of instruction files a tool loads for one session, built by walking the directory tree and concatenating what it finds.
pitfall: Reasoning about the root file alone, when the chain is what the model actually receives — so a contradiction between two files stays invisible because each file reads coherently on its own.
distractor_rationale: You edit one file at a time and read one file at a time, so the file is the natural unit of thought. Nothing in the editing workflow ever shows you the concatenated result the tool assembles.

def: The shared resolution rule that the instruction file closest to the edited file takes precedence over files higher in the tree.
deeper: In the tools that document their mechanics, 'wins' means position rather than replacement: Codex 'concatenates files from the root down' so that files closer to the working directory 'override earlier guidance because they appear later in the combined prompt,'[^S3] and Claude Code describes its equivalent as concatenation 'rather than overriding each other.'[^S5] Two consequences follow — a nested file inherits everything above it automatically, and it only wins where it explicitly says the contradicting thing.
pitfall: Reading it as replacement, so a nested file is written to restate the root rules 'because the root file is no longer active' — producing duplication that drifts out of sync.
distractor_rationale: Every override mechanism most developers know — CSS specificity, config file layering, method overriding — replaces or shadows the less specific thing. Concatenation with later-wins semantics is the unfamiliar case.

def: Precedence that comes from where text sits in an assembled prompt rather than from any mechanism that disables the losing instruction.
pitfall: Treating the nearer rule as authoritative and stopping there, when both rules are present in context and the nearer one is expected — not guaranteed — to dominate.
distractor_rationale: 'Takes precedence' is language borrowed from systems where precedence is decisive and computed. The documented behaviour is a text-ordering convention, and the phrase does not signal the difference.

def: The configurable cap on the combined size of one tool's instruction chain, past which it stops adding files.
pitfall: Assuming an oversized chain degrades gracefully, when the documented behaviour is that files stop being added — and because the chain is assembled root-first, the files dropped are the nearest and most specific ones.
distractor_rationale: Truncation usually clips the end of a document, which people picture as losing the least important part. Here the chain's end holds the most specific rules, so the cap removes exactly the files a nested layout was built to deliver.

def: A rule about a dependency between two parts of a repository, which must load for work in either part.
pitfall: Placing it in the directory it is about rather than above everything it couples, so it loads for someone editing the schema — who already knows they changed it — and is absent for the person editing the consumer that breaks.
distractor_rationale: Filing a rule with its subject is how every other kind of documentation is organised, and it produces a tidy-looking tree. The failure only shows up in the sessions where the rule was needed and silently absent.

def: The shallowest directory containing every directory whose sessions need a given rule, and therefore the correct placement for it.
pitfall: Computing it from what the rule is about rather than from which sessions need it loaded, which is the same error as the subject-matter trap and produces rules one level too deep.
distractor_rationale: The phrase sounds like a fact about the rule's topic, so people locate the subject in the tree and stop there. The calculation actually starts from a list of directories where work happens, which requires thinking about people rather than about code.

def: Attaching a rule to a file-type pattern so it loads only when the agent reads a matching file, rather than to a directory.
pitfall: Using it in a team running several tools, when glob-frontmatter and path-specific instruction files are per-vendor mechanisms — so the scoping silently does nothing for teammates on a tool that does not implement it.
distractor_rationale: It appears in the same docs as AGENTS.md support and solves a real problem nesting cannot, so it reads as part of the same standard. Nothing in the syntax signals that it is a vendor extension.

def: The part of a rule stating when it applies — before committing, after editing a directory, when adding a component.
pitfall: Omitting it and assuming the rule is understood as always-on, which makes it compete for attention on every turn and fire at none of the specific moments it was written for.
distractor_rationale: The author knows exactly when the rule matters, so the timing feels like part of the rule's meaning rather than something the text has to carry. Its absence is invisible to anyone who already has the context.

def: The part of a rule naming exactly what it concerns, in the form it appears in the repository — a path, a command, a file, a function.
pitfall: Naming a concept instead of an artifact — 'the payment code' rather than `services/payments/` or `maskCard()` — which leaves the reader to resolve the reference and reintroduces the guess.
distractor_rationale: Conceptual naming reads as clearer and more durable prose, and it survives refactors that would break a path. The cost is that resolving the reference is exactly the step where a generic prior fills the gap.

def: The part of a rule that makes compliance checkable — a command that exits clean, a file that exists, a diff that avoids a directory.
pitfall: Writing a rule whose compliance can only be assessed by judgment, so nobody can tell afterwards whether it was followed and the rule can never be tested in Lesson 6's comparison.
distractor_rationale: It is the part that feels redundant: if the action is stated, the result seems implied. It is also the hardest of the three to write, because it forces you to decide what evidence of compliance would actually look like.

def: The property of an instruction that a second person could tell, from the repository, whether it was followed.
deeper: The AAIF post draws the line with a pair: 'Follow best practices' gives an agent nothing to act on, while 'Run npm run lint after any source change' and 'do not edit files in dist/' give it 'commands, paths, and boundaries.'[^S2] Claude Code's docs give the same rewrite three times — 'Use 2-space indentation' for 'Format code properly', 'Run npm test before committing' for 'Test your changes'.[^S5] The operational test is external checkability, not how technical the sentence sounds.
pitfall: Rewriting a vague rule into a longer and more technical-sounding one that is still unfalsifiable, such as expanding 'write clean code' into a list of principles.
distractor_rationale: Vocabulary is the easiest thing to upgrade and it produces visible improvement on the page. Checkability requires knowing your own repository precisely enough to name a command or a path, which is more work than reaching for a better adjective.

def: The framing that text a model reads before acting deserves the same design effort as an interface built for a person.
pitfall: Treating instruction text as documentation to be complete about, rather than as an interface to be unambiguous about — so the file grows in coverage while individual lines stay open to interpretation.
distractor_rationale: It is a Markdown file that looks like documentation, and documentation quality is normally judged by completeness. Interfaces are judged by whether the next action is obvious, which is a different and less familiar standard for prose.

def: Changing a system so a mistake becomes impossible, rather than writing an instruction asking for it to be avoided.
pitfall: Investing in better wording for a rule that keeps being violated, when the repository could make the violation fail — a build that errors on hand-edited generated files needs no rule at all.
distractor_rationale: Rewriting a line takes two minutes and changing the build takes an afternoon, so the cheap fix is always available first. The expensive fix is the only one that removes the rule from the budget permanently.

def: Two rules that are individually clear and cannot both be followed in the same situation.
pitfall: Expecting a conflict to announce itself, when models rarely acknowledge one and simply produce one of the two behaviours — so the contradiction reads as run-to-run flakiness rather than as something you wrote.
distractor_rationale: Every other tool that encounters contradictory input errors loudly: compilers, linters, schema validators. Silent resolution is the unfamiliar behaviour, and it hides the cause in the one place nobody looks.

def: A peer-reviewed study finding that models follow the designated higher-priority instruction unreliably when two instructions conflict, even when the priority is stated explicitly.
deeper: The measured gap is the useful part: the same six models followed individual constraints at 74.8–90.8% without conflict, and followed the designated primary one at 9.6–45.8% average once a conflict was introduced.[^S7] The conflicts were deliberately minimal formatting constraints in system versus user messages on 2025-generation models — not instruction files — so the transferable claim is the mechanism, that a declared priority is weighed against everything else in context rather than disabling the losing instruction.
pitfall: Quoting its percentages as rates for AGENTS.md conflicts, when the study measured formatting constraints across system and user messages and says nothing directly about files at different directory depths.
distractor_rationale: The finding maps so neatly onto instruction-file conflicts that the difference in setting feels like a detail. A number attached to a peer-reviewed result is also more persuasive than the qualitative claim it actually supports here.

def: A model's measured tendency to favour one kind of instruction over another regardless of which was designated higher priority.
pitfall: Assuming a conflict will be resolved by the ordering you designed, when the model brings its own preferences to the resolution — with measured bias magnitudes often above 0.5 in that study's setting.
distractor_rationale: Priority is something you set, so it feels like the only input to the decision. A pre-existing preference the model brings is invisible from your side and has no representation anywhere in your file.

def: Every instruction file that loads for one directory, concatenated in load order — the text the tool actually sees.
pitfall: Auditing one file at a time and concluding the rules are consistent, when each file is internally coherent by construction and the contradiction only exists between them.
distractor_rationale: Files are the unit you edit, review, and commit, so they are the unit that feels reviewed. Assembling the chain by hand is an extra step with no tooling behind it and no prompt to do it.

def: Two individually sound rules that never mention each other but underdetermine what to do where they overlap.
pitfall: Searching for contradictions with grep and concluding the chain is clean, when this class shares no vocabulary between its two halves and can only be found by reading.
distractor_rationale: Both rules pass review individually because both are good rules, often written by different people after different incidents. There is no wrong line to find — the defect is in an intersection nobody wrote down.

def: Resolving a conflict by rewriting one rule so it no longer covers the territory the other claims.
pitfall: Reaching for stronger wording instead, which leaves both contradicting rules in context and spends emphasis that the next contested rule will then have to exceed.
distractor_rationale: Emphasis is instant and feels decisive, while narrowing requires re-reading a rule you already considered finished and admitting it was written before the exception existed.

def: An instruction file in a user's home directory that loads for all their sessions, is invisible to the repository, and differs per teammate.
pitfall: Debugging unexplained agent behaviour entirely within the repository, when a rule in a colleague's home directory is in their context and cannot be found by reading or grepping any committed file.
distractor_rationale: Everything else shaping behaviour is committed and shared, so the repository feels like a complete account of the instructions in play. A per-user layer is documented but leaves no trace anyone else can see.

def: Asking a tool which instruction files it actually read, from the directory where work happens, before drawing any conclusion from a run.
deeper: Each tool exposes this differently — Codex answers a prompt like 'List the instruction sources you loaded' and reports them in precedence order,[^S3] Amp offers `agents-md list` in its command palette,[^S4] and Claude Code lists them under Memory files in `/context`.[^S5] Running it from a subdirectory rather than the root is what makes it informative, since nested files load on demand and are the ones most likely to be silently absent.
pitfall: Skipping this and measuring a file the tool never read, which produces a clean null result that looks like evidence the file does not help.
distractor_rationale: The file is committed and visible in the editor, so its presence feels established. Loading depends on filename, launch directory, and size caps — three conditions the file's existence on disk says nothing about.

def: The spread in an agent's time, token use, and output across repeated runs of an identical task on identical inputs.
pitfall: Reading a single before/after comparison as a result, when the variation between two runs of the same condition can exceed the effect being measured and point either direction.
distractor_rationale: Identical inputs producing different outputs violates the expectation software normally sets. When the two numbers are clean and specific, the difference between them looks like a measurement rather than noise.

def: The middle value across repeated runs of one condition, used instead of a single run to keep an outlier from setting the result.
pitfall: Reporting a mean across a handful of runs, which lets one wandering run dominate the number and hides the count of bad runs that is the actual finding.
distractor_rationale: The mean is the default summary everyone reaches for and the one every spreadsheet offers first. With three runs and a heavy tail, it describes the outlier more than the condition.

def: What happens in the worst runs of a set rather than the typical ones — the wandering, re-orienting, or unrequested work an instruction file removes.
deeper: The AAIF benchmark found its most useful result here rather than in the averages: on the multi-file task the median win was only 9 to 10%, but 'two of five runs without AGENTS.md wasted time re-orienting in the repo or running an unrequested production build at the end. Every run with AGENTS.md skipped both.'[^S2] The author's advice follows from it — 'Don't optimize for the average case. Optimize for the runs where an agent would otherwise wander, reorient, or touch something it shouldn't.'
pitfall: Averaging runs into a single percentage, which dissolves a two-of-five failure rate into a small mean difference and hides the effect the file actually had.
distractor_rationale: Averages are how performance improvements are normally reported, and a percentage sounds more rigorous than a count out of three. The effect here is a change in failure frequency, which an average is the wrong instrument for.

def: An instruction naming a script, path, or process that no longer exists, and which is therefore followed into producing something nobody wants.
pitfall: Treating an outdated line as harmless clutter, when it is unambiguous and gets acted on — worse than an absent rule, which at least produces a guess that might be right.
distractor_rationale: Dead documentation is normally inert: a human reader notices the file no longer exists and moves on. An agent has no independent knowledge of what changed and executes the instruction as written.

def: A word like always, never, all, or every that extends a rule to the whole repository from a file that usually knows only one part of it.
pitfall: Leaving one in place after the exception arrives, so the rule contradicts every later nested override by construction — which is what the word means.
distractor_rationale: The universal was true when written, and nothing prompts a re-read when a new service adds its own test command. The rule keeps reading correctly to the person who wrote it, because they picture the repository as it was.

def: The number of separate instructions competing for adherence in one context.
pitfall: Counting file length in lines rather than in instructions, so a file shortened by tightening prose feels improved while the number of things being asked for is unchanged.
distractor_rationale: Length is visible and countable; density requires deciding what counts as one instruction. Editing prose produces a smaller file, which feels like progress on the metric that matters.

def: The property of a fact an agent could establish by reading the repository, which therefore does not need to be written down.
pitfall: Restating conventions the linter or the code already enforces, which is the largest source of length in files that grew by accretion and the cheapest to cut.
distractor_rationale: Writing down a convention feels like documenting it properly, and style sections are the easiest part of the file to produce. The redundancy is invisible because the file is never read beside the linter config it duplicates.

def: A nested rule that names and denies the ancestor rule it replaces, rather than merely stating its own alternative.
pitfall: Writing the nested rule as a bare statement of its own command, which leaves both commands live in context with nothing in the text choosing between them.
distractor_rationale: Naming the rule you are overriding feels redundant when the nearer file is supposed to win anyway. Precedence is positional and probabilistic, so the redundant-seeming clause is what makes the intent explicit rather than inferred.

def: The documented rule that an explicit instruction typed in conversation takes precedence over every instruction file.
pitfall: Softening a file rule to accommodate the rare case where it should not apply, when the exception can be handled in conversation on the day it arises, leaving the written rule firm.
distractor_rationale: A rule that will sometimes be wrong feels dishonest to state absolutely, so people hedge it in the file. The hedge costs adherence on the many ordinary days to buy flexibility on the rare one, which the override already provides for free.

def: The Linux Foundation body that stewards the AGENTS.md format, alongside projects including the Model Context Protocol, goose, agentgateway, and Agent2Agent.
pitfall: Reading foundation stewardship as a guarantee of stable behaviour across tools, when what it standardises is the format and the resolution rule — not how any vendor implements loading, filenames, or size caps.
distractor_rationale: Neutral governance is a real and meaningful signal about a format's durability, so it is easy to extend it to implementation consistency. The vendor divergences documented in this course all sit below the layer the foundation governs.

def: The format's self-reported count of projects using it, published without a stated method.
pitfall: Citing it as evidence the format works, when spread and effect are different claims — the AAIF post that measured behaviour opens by separating them precisely because they get conflated.
distractor_rationale: A large number from the project's own site reads as validation, and widespread adoption genuinely is evidence of something — convenience, momentum, recommendation in onboarding docs. None of those are evidence about what an agent does on a real task.

def: An instruction file below the working directory, loaded when the agent reads a file in that subtree rather than at session start.
pitfall: Placing a rule deep enough that it never loads for the sessions that needed it, since loading is driven by where work happens rather than by what the rule is about.
distractor_rationale: Deeper placement feels safer because it is more specific, and specificity is the virtue the nesting mechanism is sold on. The cost of being too deep is silent absence, which produces no error and no signal.

def: Making one set of instructions readable by a tool that reads a different filename, via an import line or a symlink.
pitfall: Bridging only the root file and leaving nested files unbridged, so a teammate's tool sees the general rules and none of the specific ones.
distractor_rationale: The root bridge is the one every migration guide shows first, and once it works the tool visibly reads instructions. Nothing signals that the subtree files are separate and still invisible.

def: Interleaving the two conditions of a comparison rather than running all of one condition first, so time-varying factors do not land on one side.
pitfall: Running the whole baseline block first and the whole treatment block after, which lets a model update, a slow API afternoon, or your own improving prompt discipline masquerade as the effect.
distractor_rationale: Batching is faster and better organised, and the sequence feels irrelevant when the prompt and commit are held fixed. The confound is in the clock, which is the one variable the setup does not control.

def: An instruction file placed inside a subdirectory, carrying rules true only of that part of the repository.
pitfall: Restating the root file's rules inside it, on the belief that the nested file replaces the ancestor — producing two copies that drift until they contradict each other.
distractor_rationale: Every override system most developers know replaces rather than appends, so a nested file feels like it must stand alone. Duplication then looks like completeness rather than a future inconsistency.

def: The instruction file at the repository root, loaded for work anywhere in the repository.
pitfall: Using it as the default home for every rule because it always loads, which reintroduces the length problem and puts rules that are false in some directories into every session.
distractor_rationale: Guaranteed availability is a real advantage and the failure mode is invisible: a rule that is wrong for one subdirectory produces a wrong action there, not an error anyone traces back to placement.

def: The sequence in which a tool concatenates discovered instruction files — root first, nearest last.
pitfall: Auditing files in the order they appear in a directory listing rather than in load order, which can make a resolved conflict look unresolved and hide a real one.
distractor_rationale: Alphabetical or filesystem order is what every tool that lists files shows you, and load order is never displayed anywhere. Reconstructing it is a manual step nothing prompts you to take.

def: The concrete, binary failure a rule was written to prevent, used as the primary signal when testing whether the rule changed behaviour.
pitfall: Measuring a proxy such as diff size instead, which can score a correct run worse — regenerating a file properly touches more lines than editing it by hand.
distractor_rationale: Proxies are continuous and feel more measurable than a yes/no observation across three runs. A percentage change also reads as more rigorous than a count, even when it is measuring the wrong thing.

def: Placing a rule in the directory the rule is about rather than in the directories whose sessions need it loaded.
pitfall: Filing a rule about the schema under the schema directory, where it loads for the person who already knows they changed it and is absent for the person whose build breaks.
distractor_rationale: Organising documents by subject is correct almost everywhere else and produces a tree that reads well. Loading is driven by where work happens, which is a fact about people rather than about topics.

def: Strengthening a rule's wording with capitals, bold, or words like ALWAYS in an attempt to make it win a conflict.
pitfall: Using it as the fix rather than as a garnish on a real fix, leaving both contradicting rules in context and spending emphasis the next contested rule will have to exceed.
distractor_rationale: It takes seconds, requires no re-reading of the rule you already considered finished, and produces a file that visibly looks more decisive. Its weakness is only observable across many runs.

def: A file produced by a build or codegen step, which should be regenerated from its source rather than edited directly.
pitfall: Writing the prohibition without naming what to edit instead, so an agent told not to touch the file has no path forward and either edits it anyway or stops.
distractor_rationale: The prohibition feels complete because it names the boundary clearly. Nothing in the directory announces where the source lives, so the agent that complies is left without a next action.

def: A tool that mechanically enforces code conventions, and therefore makes writing those conventions into an instruction file redundant.
pitfall: Documenting style rules the linter already enforces, which is usually the largest section of a long instruction file and contributes nothing an agent could not get from running the command.
distractor_rationale: Writing conventions down feels like documenting them properly, and a style section is the easiest part of the file to produce. The redundancy is invisible because nobody reads the file beside the linter config.

def: A real file in the repository pointed at from a rule, carrying the pattern more durably than a prose description of it.
pitfall: Describing a pattern in three sentences instead of naming one file that demonstrates it, which costs more lines and goes stale the moment the pattern evolves.
distractor_rationale: Prose feels self-contained and a file reference feels like passing the buck. The reference is what stays current, because it points at code somebody maintains.

def: Describing an instruction that names a desirable quality without naming an action, and which therefore cannot be complied with or checked.
pitfall: Leaving such lines in place because objecting to them sounds like arguing against the value they name, so they survive every review while changing nothing.
distractor_rationale: Nobody wants to be the person who deletes 'write secure code' from a file. The social cost of removing a line is real and the runtime cost of keeping it is invisible.

def: A repository holding several subprojects with genuinely different conventions, which is the case nesting exists to serve.
pitfall: Creating one instruction file per top-level directory because the structure suggests it, when after deletion most directories have no rules uniquely true of them.
distractor_rationale: Mirroring the directory structure looks systematic and complete. A file per directory also feels fairer to each team, which is an organisational reason rather than a reason about which rules are true where.

def: A run started with no carried-over conversation, so the instruction files are the only context shaping behaviour.
pitfall: Testing a rule in a session that already discussed the repository, where the model supplies the missing context from the conversation and the vague rule performs as well as the rewritten one.
distractor_rationale: Continuing an existing session is faster and the repository has not changed, so it feels equivalent. The accumulated conversation is exactly the context a fresh session lacks, which is the condition every real run starts in.
